newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr finds no escape from rate suspense.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr finds no escape from rate suspense.

text.p: The Australian dollar spent another session in suspended animation Tuesday as a tense market awaited developments on interest rates both here and in the U.S.

It did briefly flirt with resistance around US$0.7620 in early trade but found offshore offers, largely from U.S. investment banks, too formidable to face. Support from local exporters and European banks was equally solid under US$0.7605 and these two levels looked like caging the currency near term.
Job advertisement figures provided a taster for key labour data Thursday but suggested that while growth would pick up it might not do so with the alacrity needed to rule out a rate cut.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the currency had edged back to US$0.7610/15 from an early US$0.7615/20 having wandered between US$0.7590 and US$0.7624 through Monday's holiday-hit session.
It finished here Friday at US$0.7591/96 but did make a brief sortie to a US$0.7645 high late offshore.

On the crosses it was down at 85.95/05 yen from 87.80/90 late here Friday having been trampled by Japanese investors spooked by Monday's sharp slide in US$/yen. That contributed to a 0.3 point drop in the trade weighted index to 57.6.
US$/yen did rally today to reach 113.00 yen from a 111.80 low, which in turn lifted AUD/yen from an 85.00 yen trough.

Dollar sentiment was, as it has been for weeks now, depressed by speculation domestic interest rates were heading yet lower. Analysts are divided on whether a cut is coming or needed, but the market is taking no chances after being caught out badly by the May 23 easing.
Yields have moved sharply lower in anticipation and for periods out to three years are below those in the U.S., an event unprecedented since the dollar was floated in 1983.
The trend was encouraged by expectations the Federal Reserve would have to tighten policy to rein in runaway U.S. growth and head off inflationary pressure from a tight labour market.
Many analysts expect the Fed will move at its July 2-3 policy meeting, a complication for the RBA which also holds its monthly board meeting on July 2.
Analysts reckoned the RBA would be reluctant to ease the day after its meeting if the Fed had hiked the day before.
Equally, silence from the Fed would appear to increase the scope for the RBA to move on its own without risking too much of a backlash in the Australian dollar.
This argument taken to its logical conclusion meant the local dollar could well defy conventional wisdom and rise if the Fed hiked and fall if it did not.

The outlook for rates might be a little clearer after May labour data on Thursday, but only if outside expectations. Median forecasts are for a modest 15,000 rise in employment and a stable jobless rate of 8.7 percent, a result too mixed to advance the policy debate much.
Estimates do range from a 5,00 fall to a 25,000 rise, however, with the former likely to have the greater impact since it would be taken as a green light for an imminent easing.
Today's ANZ job ads for May offered few clues on what to expect as they were biased lower by a statistical quirk in April which delivered a record 16.7 percent rise.
Given all this, and the notorious volatility of the monthly jobs data, the market will not be taking the A$ far before then.

Also out today was a survey of Australian business which found confidence grew slightly in the June quarter with those predicting an improvement in conditions for the next six months rising to 42 percent from 35 percent in the March quarter.
Employment was expected to laf, however, unless and until GDP growth picked up to 4.0 percent and above.
Inflationary pressures were well under control with average selling prices falling for the seventh consecutive quarter and costs staying steady. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
